sections.title: Overview
sections.body:
Alcohol consumption is one of the most significant and most preventable contributors to poor health outcomes in the UK. Existing behaviour change approaches — information campaigns, counselling, GP referrals — reach a small proportion of the people who would benefit, and produce modest results in those they do reach.

This project took a different approach. Rather than trying to persuade people to drink less through information or willpower, it used Cognitive Bias Modification (CBM) to shift the underlying automatic responses that drive drinking behaviour.

sections.title: The Science
sections.body:
CBM is a clinically validated technique that retrains attentional and approach biases associated with a target substance. Heavy drinkers tend to automatically attend to alcohol cues (a glass, a pub sign, a social situation involving drink) and to have approach motivations triggered by those cues. CBM uses computer-based tasks to retrain these automatic responses at a pre-conscious level, reducing the pull of alcohol cues without requiring sustained conscious effort.

The approach was developed by Professor Paul Dolan at the London School of Economics, one of the world's leading authorities on behavioural science and wellbeing. The project brought together Telefonica Alpha, the LSE, and the BBC, whose programme "Weight for Love" provided both the research context and the initial audience.

sections.title: What We Built
sections.body:
The service was delivered digitally, making it accessible to large numbers of people without clinical contact. Users completed short CBM tasks — typically five to ten minutes — that modified their attentional and approach responses to alcohol-related stimuli over time.

The design had to make something inherently repetitive and effortful feel manageable and worth continuing. This required careful attention to session length, feedback mechanisms, and the framing of the activity in a way that felt meaningful to users rather than arbitrary.

sections.title: The Research Study
sections.body: The collaboration with the BBC enabled us to launch a large-scale research study with over 25,000 participants in the UK. This was one of the largest CBM studies conducted outside a clinical setting, and provided significant data on effectiveness, drop-off patterns, and the characteristics of users who benefited most.

sections.title: My Role
sections.body:
I led the product and design work at Telefonica Alpha, working with Professor Dolan's team at LSE on translating the clinical CBM protocols into a consumer digital product, and coordinating the BBC partnership for the research study.

The translation from clinical protocol to consumer product was the central design challenge. CBM in a clinical setting is administered by a practitioner who can motivate and monitor a patient. In a self-directed digital context, the product design has to carry all of that weight.
